about: The Student Selected Component (MBBS0078) is the Year 1 module in UCL's MBBS programme where students choose an SSC. It is taught in person in Term 2 and carries 0 credits. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue says first-year students choose an SSC to explore personal interests and build transferable skills, with options that include taught medical topics, humanities and social sciences, and that students submit their preferences at the end of Term 1. Its assessment is listed as 100% other form of assessment and varies by SSC. UCL publishes no syllabus or learning outcomes for the module as a whole, so this guide explains what the official pages confirm, labels older guidance with its year, and does not invent a syllabus.
topics: What a Student Selected Component is

notes.h: What a Student Selected Component is
notes.body:
The Student Selected Component (SSC, module code MBBS0078) is the part of UCL's MBBS Year 1 where you choose what you study, rather than following the core curriculum. UCL does not publish a syllabus for it, because the content depends on which SSC you take, so this note sets out what the official pages confirm.

What the 2026/27 catalogue entry says (last updated 10 March 2026)
- Title and code: Student Selected Component, MBBS0078, run by UCL Medical School in the Faculty of Medical Sciences and open only to students on the MBBS programme.
- Level and mode: undergraduate, FHEQ Level 4, taught in person.
- Timing: the intended teaching term is Term 2.
- Credits: 0, with no alternative credit options.
- Purpose: first-year students choose an SSC to explore personal interests and build transferable skills. Options include taught medical topics, humanities and social sciences.
- Skills named: critical thinking and problem-solving; communication and interpersonal skills; teamwork and collaboration; creative and independent thinking; writing and presentation skills.
- Teaching and assessment vary between SSCs, and generally emphasise active engagement, creative exploration, teamwork and skill development.
- Assessment is listed as 100% other form of assessment. There are no learning outcomes and no topic list on the page, which says that content varies between the SSC options.

What UCL Medical School's SSC page adds
UCL's page on Student Selected Components says SSCs are a core requirement of all undergraduate medical programmes. Their aim is to give you the chance to study additional topics, to study subjects you enjoy in more depth, and to develop one or more generic skills useful in medical practice, such as teamwork, essay writing and research. It also says that SSCs let students demonstrate required competences while choosing an area that interests them. The page does not list the options; look for the current list on the Year 1 SSC Moodle course.

Why it matters
Although it carries 0 credits, UCL's Year 1 programme page lists it as a Year 1 module and the Mark Scheme requires the portfolio for progression to include marks for SSCs (see the later note).

Exam tips: there is no content to revise for a written paper. Treat the SSC as a piece of coursework and teamwork in a subject you chose; the best preparation is turning up, engaging and planning your written work early.

This note separates what is confirmed for 2026–27 from what was described for an earlier year, so you know how much to rely on each.

Confirmed for 2026–27
- Term: the catalogue gives Term 2 as the intended teaching term.
- Timing in the week: the summary table in UCL's 2026–27 overall timetable (May 2026 version) shows Year 1 SSCs on Thursday afternoons.
- Choosing: the catalogue says students submit their SSC preferences at the end of Term 1.
- The options: the catalogue says options include taught medical topics, humanities and social sciences. Look for the current list on the Year 1 SSC Moodle course.

How Year 1 SSCs were run in 2024–25 (older edition, background only)
UCL's 2024–25 management guide for SSC leads, dated March 2024, described the arrangements for that year. They may have changed, so check the current Moodle course.
- Year 1 SSCs ran as one 8-week block from January to March on Thursday afternoons.
- Each session lasted three hours, but not all of it was face-to-face. Part or all of some afternoons was given for research and preparing coursework or presentations, with more preparation done in private study.
- Groups were around 35 students.
- Leads had to give students a description, aims and learning outcomes, a weekly timetable, assessment details and marking criteria, and had to give written objectives and a programme in the first session.

A possible future change
A UCL MBBS newsletter (March 2026) mentions, in a Curriculum Review 27/28 update, that the SSC will take place after end-of-year examinations. The sentence names no year group, but it sits under a 'Focus on Year 1' heading about the revised Year 1 planned for 2027/28. The 2026–27 timetable still shows Year 1 SSCs on Thursday afternoons, so treat the newsletter as a sign of future change, not of this year's arrangements.

What to do with this
- Check the current SSC Moodle course for your allocated SSC's timetable, location and requirements.
- Put the sessions and every deadline in your calendar as soon as you know them.
- If your SSC has preparation between sessions, plan time for it in your weekly schedule, since Thursday afternoons alone may not cover it.

Exam tips: because SSC arrangements vary between options and years, trust your own SSC's written objectives and programme (which the 2024–25 guide said leads must provide in the first session) over any general description, including this one.

UCL's pages on SSC assessment are limited, so this note separates the confirmed 2026–27 position from the 2024–25 guidance. Always check the current SSC Moodle course for the rules that apply to you.

Confirmed for 2026–27
- The catalogue lists the assessment as 100% other form of assessment, and says teaching and assessment vary by SSC.
- UCL's 2026–27 Mark Scheme and Boards of Examiners document says that to progress from Year 1 to Year 2 you must complete the full prescribed course of study with sign-off for required modules, and submit a portfolio containing marks for all required coursework and student selected components. The requirements are on the Year Moodle site, and each module must be completed and graded.

What the 2024–25 management guide said (older edition)
- To progress, students had to complete the SSC to a satisfactory standard, which covered coursework, attendance and engagement.
- Each SSC had to include individual written work submitted through Turnitin. An essay alone was limited to 1500 words, and an essay combined with another method was recommended, for example a 1000-word essay with a 15-minute individual presentation.
- Word limits had about 10% leeway; work outside the range received a grade of D.
- Grades ran from A to F, without modifiers such as A+ or B-.
- Final grades did not count toward end-of-year exam marks but formed part of overall achievement.
- The standard submission deadline was 5pm on the due date, and extensions could only be approved by the Divisional Tutor.
- If a student failed, the lead had to offer an alternative assessment, and a second-attempt grade was capped at D.
- Students who failed because of undocumented poor attendance were not eligible for reassessment and might have to take a year away.
- Similarity scores of 15–25% on written work were described as a concern, and scores above 30% as serious plagiarism requiring the work to be redone on a different topic.

What to take from this
- Attend every session, and if you cannot, tell your SSC lead and the year team and document the reason.
- Start the written work early and check the word limit and format for your SSC.
- Write in your own words and reference sources, since similarity checks are used.
- Read the marking criteria your SSC lead publishes.

Exam tips: the SSC is not examined in an AKT. Aim to meet the published criteria, submit on time and keep copies of everything you submit for your portfolio.

The SSC is one of the few places in Year 1 where you get a say in what you study. Use that choice carefully. This note offers practical advice built on what UCL's pages say; it is not a UCL requirement list.

Choosing
- Preferences are submitted at the end of Term 1, according to the catalogue. Check the Year 1 SSC Moodle course for the list of options and for the deadline.
- UCL's 2024–25 guide for SSC leads said students were encouraged to rank their preferences from across the wide variety of SSCs on offer, so avoid listing only options similar to one another.
- The catalogue says options include taught medical topics, humanities and social sciences. Think about whether you want depth in a subject you like, or to try something different from the core curriculum.
- Look at the skills the catalogue names (critical thinking, communication, teamwork, creative and independent thinking, writing and presentation) and ask which you most want to develop.
- Check how the SSC is assessed and the weekly workload before you rank it.

Preparing
- Once allocated, read the SSC's description, aims, learning outcomes, timetable and marking criteria. UCL's 2024–25 guide said leads must provide these.
- Plan time for preparation and coursework around Thursday afternoons, bearing in mind the 2024–25 guide said some afternoons were partly given to research and preparation.
- Work out the submission method and deadlines early. In 2024–25 individual written work was submitted through Turnitin.
- If you have a long-term illness, disability or other circumstance that affects attendance or deadlines, speak to the year team and use UCL's support processes early.

Making the most of it
- Treat teamwork sessions as practice for clinical teams: listen, share the work fairly and give feedback kindly.
- Keep evidence of what you did and a copy of your submitted work, since the portfolio must contain marks for SSCs.
- Reflect on what you learned and how it connects to your wider medical education.

Exam tips: do not leave the written work to the last week. A first outline early on, checked against the marking criteria, is the best way to meet the standard and the deadline.

questions.q: According to UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue entry for the Student Selected Component, when do students submit their SSC preferences?
options: After the Year 1 Applied Knowledge Tests
During the Introduction and Orientation week
questions.why: The catalogue entry says students submit their SSC preferences at the end of Term 1, ahead of the Term 2 teaching. The orientation week at the start of the year is too early, since students have not yet seen the options. The start of Term 3 would be after the Term 2 teaching, and waiting until after the Applied Knowledge Tests confuses the end-of-year summative papers with the SSC choice, which has to be made before the SSC is taught.

questions.q: UCL's 2024–25 management guide for Year 1 SSCs (an older edition) described how final SSC grades were reported. Which statement matches it?
options: Grades ran from A to F, did not count toward end-of-year exam marks, but formed part of overall achievement
Grades were reported as distinction, merit or pass
Grades were reported as pass or fail only
Grades were reported as percentages and added to the Applied Knowledge Test marks
questions.why: The 2024–25 guide said grades ran from A to F, did not count toward end-of-year exam marks, and formed part of overall achievement. A pass or fail only system is not what the guide described. Adding SSC marks to the Applied Knowledge Tests would contradict the statement that they do not count toward exam marks. Distinction, merit or pass bands were not used for SSC grades; the only merit-type Year 1 award in the Mark Scheme is the Certificate of Merit, which is based on examination scores.

questions.q: Which statement about the purpose of Student Selected Components matches UCL's SSC page and the module catalogue?
options: They are limited to taught medical topics
They are a way to study extra topics, study topics in more depth, or build skills such as teamwork and presentation
They replace core clinical placements in Year 1
They are open only to students who want to intercalate
questions.why: UCL says SSCs give students the chance to study additional topics, study subjects in more depth and develop generic skills such as teamwork and essay writing, and the catalogue names writing and presentation skills. They do not replace core placements, which are taught in other modules. SSCs are a core requirement of undergraduate medical programmes for all students, not an option reserved for those planning to intercalate. The catalogue also says options include humanities and social sciences, so they are not limited to taught medical topics.

questions.q: Explain what is confirmed about how Year 1 SSCs are assessed and recorded in 2026–27, what an older guide said about 2024–25, and why you should check the current SSC Moodle course.
markScheme: 2026/27 catalogue: assessment is 100% other form of assessment and varies by SSC
2026–27 Mark Scheme: the progression portfolio must contain marks for required coursework and SSCs; requirements are on the Year Moodle site

Check Moodle because arrangements can change between years and vary by SSC
questions.modelAnswer: For 2026–27, the module catalogue lists SSC assessment as 100% other form of assessment and says it varies between SSCs. The Mark Scheme says the Year 1 to Year 2 progression portfolio must contain marks for all required coursework and student selected components, with the requirements listed on the Year Moodle site. UCL's older 2024–25 guide for SSC leads described a satisfactory standard covering coursework, attendance and engagement, individual written work submitted through Turnitin, and grades from A to F that did not count toward end-of-year exam marks. Because that guide is from an earlier year and each SSC sets its own criteria, you should check the current SSC Moodle course and your SSC's own written objectives and marking criteria.
